newsitem.title: FINLAND: FINNISH GOVT LEAVES ROOM FOR TAX CUT TO CAP WAGES.
newsitem.headline: FINNISH GOVT LEAVES ROOM FOR TAX CUT TO CAP WAGES.

text.p: The Finnish government said on Friday that its 1998 state budget proposal included income tax cuts and an option to lower income taxes further to promote a moderate incomes settlement in talks this autumn.

The budget proposal included a two percent inflation adjustement to income taxes which would lower the total income tax burden by about 750 million markka next year, but a moderate pay deal could bring additional tax relief, it said.
The labour market organisations are preparing to start talks on a pay deal for 1998, and most key organisations aim to reach a broad national agreement covering all sectors.
"When deciding on (further) tax cuts, promoting employment and controlling inflation will be taken into account," the government said in a statement.
There would be a shift in taxation from income to energy use, and Finance Minister Sauli Niinisto said the bulk of the energy tax hike would hit industry.
"It will hit industry and private consumption, but more the industry since it will also benefit from the same decisions," Niinisto told a news conference.
Prime Minister Paavo Lipponen said this statement was not a threat to the labour market organisations, but an offer.

"At the moment it is difficult to say what will happen if a comprehensive deal would not be reached," Lipponen said. "It is of course possible that income taxation could be used to promote employment in any case."
"It is possible that even if a broad deal cannot be reached, the low-inflation policy could be maintained with branch settlements, however apparently better in a broad deal," Lipponen said.
Lipponen also said labour market parties should seek more flexible agreements to promote employment.
"Reponsibility for employment is now quite far in the hands of the labour market lobbies," Lipponen said.
The budget proposal included the following proposals on taxation:
- A two percent inflation adjustment of income taxes, easing income taxation by some 750 million markka.
- Reducing tax deductions of commuting costs by raising the limit of non-deductable expenses to 3,000 markka from 2,500.
- Limiting developing areas tax exemptions to the small and medium size corporate sector.
- Moving some of municipalities' and the church's corporate tax revenue to state coffers for a total of 830 million markka next year.

- Introducing only two value-added-tax rates below the main rate to comply with EU rules; the main VAT rate will remain 22 percent and the current 12 percent and six percent rates will become eight percent. Impact: 100 million loss of revenue.
- Raising petrol tax by 20 penni per litre and diesel tax by 15 penni per litre.
- A 50 percent tax ease on natural gas to become permanent, and taxation on wood and wood-based fuels to be lowered. These will be financed with an overall rise in the energy tax.
- Electricity tax on railways and tramway traffic to be removed.
- Tax on wines and mild alcohol products to be lowered by an average of 17 percent.
- Government prepares to abandon sweetener tax in 1999.
